runs.answer: A CodeAgent is not safe in a public Space because it can be used to access sensitive information such as environment variables and OAuth client secrets. The CodeAgent interpreter filters names but hands out real objects, which can be exploited by an attacker to walk attributes inside C and access sensitive data. This is a known weakness of local executors. To mitigate this, it is recommended to use a ToolCallingAgent instead, which only returns JSON and does not allow model-written code to run. Additionally, it is important to implement proper OAuth and quota management to prevent abuse. runs.answer: Changing the temperature affected the dummy agent's answers by altering the likelihood of the model sampling different tokens. At temperature 0, the model always chooses the top token, resulting in the same output every time. At temperature 1, the model samples from its real probabilities, allowing for some variation in the output. At temperature 2, the probabilities are flattened, making less likely tokens more probable and resulting in more diverse and potentially incorrect outputs. This is evident in the experiment where the model was run multiple times with different temperatures, resulting in different outputs, including invented observations and final answers. Source: 1.1-LL-dummy-agent-temperature (https://github.com/MArchMondello/hf-AI-agents-course/blob/main/brain/1.1-LL-dummy-agent-temperature.md)

runs.answer: Byte-pair encoding splits words into tokens by identifying common subwords or character sequences within a vocabulary. It works by first identifying individual characters as the base tokens, then iteratively merging the most frequent adjacent pairs of characters or character sequences to form new tokens. This process continues until a predefined vocabulary size is reached. The resulting tokens can be subwords (smaller units of words) or full words, depending on their frequency in the training data. This allows the model to efficiently represent both common and rare words, as well as words that did not appear in the training data (out-of-vocabulary words), by breaking them down into their constituent subwords. The process involves two halves: finding the right note and then finding the right part of that note. This is achieved through the use of BM25F, a ranking function that takes into account the rarity of words (idf) and the length of the note. The agent reads the notes section by section, using the `topic` parameter to focus on the most relevant parts. This approach helps to avoid common errors such as a common word outranking a rare one, a long note always winning or losing, and the right note but wrong answer.
